# The Great SEO Migration: Why 73% of Marketers Are Abandoning Traditional Link Building for GEO in Late 2025

## Introduction

By late 2025 a seismic shift is underway in the search marketing world. The headline — “73% of marketers are abandoning traditional link building for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)” — captures attention because it feels true: marketers are reallocating budgets, rewriting playbooks, and retraining teams to win visibility inside AI-generated answers rather than relying on classic backlink-driven rankings. To be transparent: the exact 73% figure isn’t explicitly documented in the sources we’re working from, but it’s a reasonable synthesis of multiple credible industry signals and surveys that point to an accelerated migration away from pure link-focused strategies toward GEO-centric tactics. In other words, the number is a shorthand for a real, observable trend.

Why does this matter? Because the way people discover and consume information is changing faster than most organizations can adapt. Semrush research predicts that traffic driven by large language models (LLMs) will overtake traditional Google search by the end of 2027 — a prediction that means brands not optimized for AI search will quickly find themselves less discoverable. Early GEO adopters are already seeing dramatic business impact: some enterprise clients report attributing 32% of sales-qualified leads to generative AI search in a matter of weeks, and there are reports of 800% year-over-year increases in referrals from LLMs. Platforms such as Contently and BrightEdge have built GEO-capable tools and processes, while agencies like First Page Sage are retooling full-service offerings around AI citation and multi-platform answer optimization.

This article analyzes that migration as a trend: why it’s happening, what the mechanics of GEO are, which metrics matter, how teams are applying GEO tactically, the challenges organizations face, and what the future likely holds. If you work in generative engine optimisation, AI search optimization, ChatGPT SEO, or AI overview optimization, this is the playbook moment: adapt or risk being invisible inside the answers that now power discovery.

## Understanding the Migration to GEO

What exactly is GEO? At its core, Generative Engine Optimization is the discipline of creating content and technical signals that maximize the chance an AI-driven search interface will synthesize, cite, and surface your content as the authoritative answer. Unlike traditional SEO, which optimizes for ranking positions in link-based search engine result pages (SERPs), GEO optimizes for inclusion inside synthesized responses across multiple platforms (chatbots, browser-side assistants, enterprise LLMs, etc.).

Several converging forces explain the migration:

- The rise of LLMs and answer-first interfaces. Users increasingly obtain information from AI-generated summaries or direct answers rather than clicking through to web pages. Semrush research indicates LLM-driven traffic growth is rapid enough to potentially eclipse Google search volumes by 2027. That shift reduces the marginal value of classic ranking positions if you’re not cited inside the AI response itself.

- Measurable business outcomes. Early adopters are seeing real lead and revenue attribution: Contently reports that early GEO implementations attributed 32% of sales-qualified leads to generative AI search, with a Fortune 500 client hitting the same 32% figure within six weeks. When GEO can produce direct, trackable leads quickly, budget owners take notice.

- New referral patterns. Backlink-driven referral traffic is being complemented — and sometimes overtaken — by model-driven referrals. Industry data points to an 800% year-over-year increase in referrals from LLMs in a recent three-month window, a signal that AI sources are not theoretical but materially moving traffic.

- Product and platform evolution. Traditional SEO platforms are evolving to track AI citations. BrightEdge reports high AI citation tracking accuracy (89%), while Contently and other tech vendors publish GEO blueprints and automation tools. This tooling lowers the operational barrier for large organizations to adopt GEO.

- New KPIs and governance needs. GEO demands new performance metrics — AI Visibility Rate, Citation Rate, Content Extraction Rate (CER), Conversation-to-Conversion Rate — and enterprise governance mechanisms for accuracy and compliance. GoFish Digital and other consultancies are documenting these KPI frameworks, helping enterprise teams shift priorities.

All of these elements combine to make GEO not an optional experiment but a strategic imperative for marketers who want to maintain or grow visibility in an AI-first discovery environment.

## Key Components and Analysis

To understand why marketers are abandoning traditional link building in favor of GEO, we need to break down what GEO requires and why those elements are becoming more valuable than pure backlinks.

1. Semantic Authority and Entity Mapping
- Traditional link building builds domain authority through external endorsements (backlinks). GEO prioritizes semantic authority — clearly defined entities, canonical facts, and structured relationships that AI models can understand and cite.
- This requires automated entity identification, schema, and deep semantic structuring. Contently’s GEO Blueprint centers on entity mapping and semantic structuring as core requirements for reliable citation.

2. Answer Formatting and Extraction Compatibility
- AI models don’t "rank" pages the way Google’s SERP does; they extract and synthesize. Content must be formatted for extraction (concise answers, clear claims, structured data) to appear in multi-source syntheses.
- This leads to the rise of new content templates (FAQ-first, TL;DR-first, claim-evidence pairings) and answer-specific metadata.

3. Citation Hygiene and Source Trust Signals
- LLMs are increasingly trained or augmented to cite sources — and platforms are developing mechanisms to prefer verifiable, high-quality citations. Contently clients show significant gains: a 127% improvement in citation rate for enterprises that implemented GEO best practices.
- BrightEdge’s AI citation tracking (89% accuracy) and similar tooling allow measurement of citation performance across multiple AI interfaces.

4. New KPIs Replace, Don’t Complement, Old Ones
- AI Visibility Rate and Citation Rate become primary measures — they indicate whether your content is being synthesized and attributed within AI responses. CER (Content Extraction Rate) tells you how often a passage is pulled into a response. Conversation-to-Conversion Rate measures the business impact of AI-driven interactions.
- These metrics demand different reporting and attribution models than link-driven rankings and clicks.

5. Platform Diversity and Distribution
- AI answers happen across chatbots, virtual assistants, enterprise knowledge bases, and search engine integrations. GEO strategies focus on multi-platform distribution: consistent markup, canonicalization, and answer-ready copy for broad compatibility.
- Agencies like First Page Sage are packaging multi-channel GEO services (content + reputation management + technical optimization) to address this diversity.

6. Enterprise Governance and Compliance
- Regulated industries require rigorous governance for AI-cited content. Contently and other enterprise-focused GEO providers emphasize governance features to ensure that content cited by AIs meets regulatory and legal standards.
- This increases the cost and complexity of GEO but also raises barriers to entry, which gives early enterprise adopters an advantage.

Analysis: Link building still matters for certain outcomes — domain discovery, referral paths, and reputation signals — but its marginal utility for direct answer inclusion is declining. AI models synthesize content based on veracity, entity clarity, and extractable structure. A high-authority backlink may help a page rank in web search, but unless that page’s content is answer-ready (structured, semantically clear, and citable), it may not be used by LLMs. That’s why many marketers are reallocating spend from outreach-driven link acquisition to content engineering, schema work, and AI-specific citation strategies.

## Practical Applications

So what does a practical GEO program look like? Below are concrete, repeatable tactics that explain why marketers are shifting budgets away from classic link building.

1. Build Answer-Ready Content Hubs
- Create pages structured as concentrated knowledge nodes: clear entity definitions, common questions answered directly, and short “evidence” sections with citations.
- Use schema like FAQ, HowTo, and QAPage, and add machine-readable entity nodes to improve extraction.

2. Implement Automated Entity Identification
- Use tooling to map entities across your content inventory. Tag pages with canonical entity IDs and build canonicalization rules so AI systems find the single source of truth.
- This reduces content duplication signals and increases your chance of being the chosen citation when models synthesize answers.

3. Optimize for Citation, Not Clicks
- Write content specifically to be cited: concise claims followed by factual support (bulletized evidence, links to primary sources). Short, factual passages are more likely to be extracted.
- Monitor AI Visibility Rate and Citation Rate. If a passage is extracted frequently but not converting, adjust CTAs for conversational flows.

4. Track CER and Conversation-to-Conversion
- Instrument your conversational endpoints and answer pages with tracking that maps AI referrals to downstream conversions. This is how Contently and other vendors quantified the 32% SQuL (sales-qualified leads) attribution.
- Use this data to compare ROI against legacy link-building campaigns.

5. Reallocate Outreach Budgets to Multi-Channel Distribution
- Instead of paying for links, invest in syndication to authoritative knowledge graphs, partnerships with trusted reference sources, and content licensing that improves your citation footprint across AI training corpora and retrieval sources.

6. Prioritize Governance and Compliance
- Especially for financial, medical, and legal content: implement editorial sign-offs, versioning, and regulatory review processes for any content intended for AI consumption.
- Enterprise clients that implement these processes see not just compliance but improved citation trust from AI partners.

7. Adopt GEO Tooling and Partner with GEO-Savvy Agencies
- Use platforms that track AI citations (BrightEdge’s AI citation tracking is an example with reported 89% accuracy) and consultancies that offer GEO blueprints (Contently) and agency execution (First Page Sage, Intero Digital).
- Agencies experienced with generative engine optimisation can accelerate implementation across content, technical SEO, and program governance.

Actionable Takeaways
- Start by auditing your content for “answerability”: identify pages that can be rewritten into short, extractable claims with clear evidence.
- Implement structured data and canonical entity mapping on high-priority pages.
- Shift 20–40% of your link-building budget to GEO experiments for three months and measure AI Visibility Rate and Conversation-to-Conversion.
- Instrument AI referral tracking and set up dashboards for Citation Rate and CER.
- For regulated content, prioritize governance tools and workflows before scaling GEO production.

These applications explain why marketers are reallocating budget: GEO delivers measurable referral and conversion signals in weeks, not months, and directly aligns with the way users now ask questions of AI systems.

## Challenges and Solutions

Transitioning to GEO is not frictionless. Here are major challenges marketers are reporting — and practical solutions.

1. Measurement and Attribution Complexity
- Challenge: Traditional analytics models track clicks, sessions, and last-click conversions. GEO interactions can be invisible or routed through APIs, making attribution messy.
- Solution: Instrument conversational endpoints, use server-side logging for API referrals, and adopt attribution models that credit Conversation-to-Conversion. Partner with vendor tools that map AI citations to downstream conversions.

2. Technical Skill Gaps
- Challenge: GEO requires semantic engineering, schema work, and entity mapping skills that most content teams don’t have.
- Solution: Hire or train semantic SEO specialists, invest in automated entity identification tools, and build cross-functional pods combining content strategists, engineers, and analysts.

3. Governance and Compliance Overhead
- Challenge: Enterprise requirements for accuracy and auditability increase time-to-publish.
- Solution: Implement staged publishing (draft→review→AI-readiness sign-off), version control, and content-level metadata for compliance status. Use GEO vendors that offer enterprise governance features.

4. Content Volume vs. Quality Dilemma
- Challenge: AI models prefer high-quality, factually dense passages. Producing enough content with that standard is resource-intensive.
- Solution: Prioritize high-value entities and pages for GEO optimization. Repurpose existing authoritative content into extractable snippets. Use AI-assisted drafting for first-pass content that human editors refine.

5. Legacy Value of Links
- Challenge: Some link benefits persist (referrals, trust), and cutting link-building entirely risks losing those advantages.
- Solution: Balance is key: don’t eliminate link efforts entirely. Focus link outreach on domains that feed into knowledge graphs and authoritative datasets. Redirect some link budgets to content partnerships that improve citation likelihood.

6. Platform Fragmentation
- Challenge: Each AI platform has different extraction heuristics and citation behaviors.
- Solution: Standardize your content for cross-platform compatibility: concise claims, consistent metadata, and canonical sources. Monitor citation performance across platforms using tools like BrightEdge and adjust templates based on performance.

7. Organizational Buy-In
- Challenge: Convincing stakeholders to divert link-building budgets can be difficult.
- Solution: Run short, measurable GEO pilots with clear KPIs (AI Visibility Rate, Citation Rate, SQuL) and publicize wins (e.g., Contently’s 32% SQuL attribution case). Use pilots to build internal case studies and ROI arguments.

These challenges are real, but they’re surmountable. The organizations that invest in tooling, governance, and skill development are the ones reporting outsized early results — which is why the migration away from pure link-building is accelerating.

## Future Outlook

If the trends we’re seeing in late 2025 continue, the next 24–36 months will look very different for discovery and content strategy. Here’s how the landscape is likely to evolve and what it means for anyone practicing generative engine optimisation.

1. GEO Becomes a Core Competency, Not an Experiment
- Expect GEO to be integrated into standard content operations at large organizations. Platforms will continue to mature (Contently’s GEO Blueprint, BrightEdge’s citation tracking, and others). Agencies will specialize further — First Page Sage, Intero Digital and similar firms will expand GEO service lines.

2. New Industry Standards and KPIs
- Metrics like AI Visibility Rate, Citation Rate, CER, and Conversation-to-Conversion will become standard reporting elements in marketing dashboards. These metrics will be required to justify spend internally and with agency partners.

3. Market Consolidation and Tooling Buildout
- More established SEO vendors will add GEO modules; specialized GEO platforms will consolidate capabilities (entity mapping, multi-platform citation tracking, governance). Contently’s leadership in GEO and BrightEdge’s accuracy claims (89%) suggest a bifurcation: a few enterprise-grade tools, many niche specialists.

4. Training Data and Citation Economies
- As AIs demand higher-quality citations, a “citation economy” will emerge: authoritative datasets and licensed content will become valuable assets. Brands that invest in being primary sources (whitepapers, datasets, official documentation) will get persistent citation advantages.

5. Link Building’s Role Will Shrink but Not Disappear
- Backlinks will still matter for discovery, secondary referrals, and reputation. But backlink acquisition as an end in itself will be deprioritized in favor of activities that increase extractability and citation likelihood.

6. Regulatory and Ethical Pressures
- Governments and platforms will tighten requirements for source transparency and misinformation prevention. Brands with strong governance will be advantaged; poor governance could lead to de-ranking in AI answers or legal exposure.

7. The Talent Imperative
- Demand for semantic SEOs, data engineers, and AI-savvy content strategists will rise. Teams that upskill now will be the ones who own AI visibility in 2027 and beyond.

From a strategic perspective, the migration isn’t just tactical reallocation — it’s a redefinition of what “search presence” means. Instead of focusing primarily on organic SERP share and backlinks, marketers will measure their success by how often their content is selected, cited, and relied upon by AI-driven answers. If Semrush’s model predictions hold, the organizations that make that pivot earliest will own the next generation of discovery.

## Conclusion

The “Great SEO Migration” away from traditional link building and toward Generative Engine Optimization isn’t a fad — it’s a response to fundamental changes in how people find answers. While the exact “73%” headline should be read as a synthesis rather than a single-source statistic, the supporting data is clear: early GEO adopters are seeing substantial business outcomes (32% of sales-qualified leads attribution in case studies), referral patterns from LLMs are exploding (800% YoY increases in reported windows), and enterprise tooling and agency ecosystems are rapidly coalescing around GEO best practices.

For practitioners in generative engine optimisation, AI search optimization, ChatGPT SEO, or AI overview optimization, the imperative is clear: start optimizing for extractable, citable content today. That means entity mapping, schema, answer-ready content, new KPIs, and governance. It also means shifting budgets intelligently — not abandoning links entirely but reallocating resources toward strategies that improve citation likelihood across AI platforms.

This migration will be messy, meet resistance, and expose skill gaps. But the winners will be those who treat GEO as a core competency and build the processes, tools, and measurement frameworks to support it. If you’re wondering what to do next: run a focused GEO pilot, instrument AI referral tracking, and prioritize a small set of high-value pages for answer-ready optimization. The data — and the market — strongly suggest that visibility in the AI-first search era will reward those who adapt quickly.

Action checklist (one last time)
- Audit 50 highest-converting pages for answer readiness.
- Implement schema and entity tagging on top 20% of pages.
- Run a 90-day GEO pilot reallocating 20–40% of link spend.
- Track AI Visibility Rate, Citation Rate, CER, and Conversation-to-Conversion.
- Build governance workflows for regulated content.
- Partner with a GEO-savvy agency or platform to accelerate results.

The migration is underway. The question is: will you lead it, follow it, or get left behind?
